additional_context:
Council feedback from model_reviewer:
- proposed_definition.kinematic_profile.primary_joint_actions[ankle_joint/plantarflexion]: Listing ankle plantarflexion as a primary joint action makes soleus 1.0 and medial and lateral gastrocnemius 0.8 and 0.7 primary movers, equal to the quadriceps and gluteus maximus. The assumptions call this only a modest contribution. In a deep squat the knee is heavily flexed, which puts the gastrocnemii at a mechanical disadvantage. Ankle motion is mainly dorsiflexion and a small plantarflexion on the rise, so the calf pattern is overstated. Suggested correction: Remove ankle plantarflexion from primary_joint_actions. Represent the soleus contribution through stabilization demands such as ankle_stability or postural_sway_control, so the calves are stabilizers or low-weight contributors rather than primary movers.
- proposed_definition.kinematic_profile.stabilization_demands[grip, wrist_stability]: The frames show the bar resting on the upper back with the hands only steadying it at the sides. The hands do not carry the load, unlike a deadlift or carry. The grip and wrist_stability demands engage about 50 hand and forearm muscles (FDP 0.35, wrist extensors and flexors up to 0.28, thenar and interossei muscles). That is an unsupported and materially wrong pattern for a back squat. Suggested correction: Drop grip and wrist_stability, or justify them with evidence that the hands bear significant load. If the lifter does not actively grip against load, the forearm and hand muscles should be zero.
- proposed_definition.kinematic_profile.stabilization_demands[shoulder_position_hold]: The bar load acts on the back through the traps and rear shoulders and is not resisted by isometric shoulder flexion. Because of this demand, the clavicular deltoid gets 0.35 and the pectoralis major heads and coracobrachialis get low nonzero values. The justification, that the upper arms are held abducted and externally rotated, does not describe a load acting on the arm from further down the limb. Suggested correction: Remove shoulder_position_hold, or replace it with a demand that matches the real shoulder-girdle task of holding the bar shelf.
- proposed_definition.kinematic_profile.stabilization_demands: The main upper-body task of the squat is retracting and bracing the scapulae to create the shelf that supports the bar. No scapular demand is present, so the trapezius (transverse and ascending parts) and the rhomboids are explicit zeros. The tracer therefore shows hand and deltoid involvement but no scapular retractors. Suggested correction: Add scapular_retraction_stability or scapular_stabilization to represent the upper-back bar support, and remove the unsupported hand and shoulder-hold demands.

assumptions: The bar is a back squat on the upper back (shoulders slightly below the neck), not a front squat, as shown in both frames.
The exertion phase is the ascent. It is driven by knee extension and hip extension, with a bilateral stance and both feet fixed on the floor.

Ankle plantarflexion is omitted as a primary action per review. The knees are deeply flexed, which puts the gastrocnemii at a mechanical disadvantage, so calf involvement is carried as soleus stabilization through postural_stabilization.
The hands only steady the bar and do not bear load, so grip, wrist_stability and shoulder_position_hold are omitted.
The upper-back bar shelf is represented by scapular_retraction_stability.
Heavy loaded bracing and spinal-extensor demand are assumed, so anti_flexion_spine and intra_abdominal_pressure are included.
Stance is shoulder width with toes slightly out. Rotation and frontal-plane actions are not treated as primary.
Bar position (high or low) is not distinguished and is assumed not to change the primary joint actions.
classification_reasons: Both frames and the instructions show a bilateral barbell back squat. The bar rests on the upper back, and the lifter descends by flexing the knees and hips and then rises by extending them.
Knee extension and hip extension are available in the tracer vocabulary, along with the stabilization demands needed for this lift.
Variant, laterality and kinetic chain are clear from the frames. Any bar-height difference does not materially change the joint actions.

instructions: This exercise is best performed inside a squat rack for safety purposes. To begin, first set the bar on a rack just above shoulder level. Once the correct height is chosen and the bar is loaded, step under the bar and place the back of your shoulders (slightly below the neck) across it.
Hold on to the bar using both arms at each side and lift it off the rack by first pushing with your legs and at the same time straightening your torso.

Step away from the rack and position your legs using a shoulder-width medium stance with the toes slightly pointed out. Keep your head up at all times and maintain a straight back. This will be your starting position.

Begin to slowly lower the bar by bending the knees and sitting back with your hips as you maintain a straight posture with the head up. Continue down until your hamstrings are on your calves. Inhale as you perform this portion of the movement.
Begin to raise the bar as you exhale by pushing the floor with the heel or middle of your foot as you straighten the legs and extend the hips to go back to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
